title: A good opponent
hook: difficulties show who we are, like a trainer pairing you with a rough young wrestler (Discourses 1.24)
carry: what is this making of me

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was money-changer: test each thought before you spend it. Your line was an impression is a coin someone has passed you.

In a boxing gym, the coach looks over the new kid and pairs him, on purpose, not with the easiest partner but with someone a little rougher, a little stronger, someone who makes him sweat and sometimes puts him down. He goes home sore and annoyed. A few months on, he moves differently. Epictetus took that gym wisdom and pointed it at the hardest things in life.
screen: `THE COACH PAIRS HIM ROUGHER.` → `SORE AND ANNOYED.` → `A FEW MONTHS ON.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-four, on how to struggle with circumstances. It opens with a short line: it's difficulties that show what people are. Then the picture. When a difficulty lands on you, Epictetus says, remember that God, like a wrestling trainer, has paired you with a rough young opponent. Why? So that you can become an Olympic champion, and that doesn't happen without sweat. Then something bold. No one, he tells his student, has ever been handed a better difficulty than yours, if you're willing to use it the way an athlete uses a tough sparring partner. Notice what he's not saying. Not that the difficulty is good in itself, or that you deserved it, or that suffering is secretly pleasant. The opponent is rough. It hurts. What he changes is the question. Instead of, why is this happening to me, he asks: what is this making of me? A sparring partner isn't your enemy, even when he puts you on the mat. He's how you find out what you've got, and how you get more of it. For the Stoics, the trainer is God, the reason that runs the world. Some readers keep that, and some keep only the gym. Either way, a hard conversation, a setback at work, a stubborn habit can be read as the partner your training needed.
screen: `DIFFICULTIES SHOW WHAT PEOPLE ARE.` · `THE TRAINER PAIRS YOU ROUGH.` · `NO BETTER DIFFICULTY THAN YOURS.` · `WHAT IS THIS MAKING OF ME?` · then, large: `A GOOD OPPONENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one difficulty you're facing now, and picture it not as a wall but as a rough young opponent across the mat. What is it working in you: patience, courage, honesty, endurance? Step onto the mat in your mind, not happy about it, just willing; you don't have to win today.
Sparring partner. Epictetus' name for hardship: the rough partner a trainer chooses for you, so you find out what you've got, and grow it.
Your line: what is this making of me. The opponent is rough, and the training is real. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a difficulty as a training partner, asking what virtue it calls on, a habit drawn from this chapter's wrestling image.
